title: Developmental Delay — Red Flags & Evaluation
sources: Critical Vector — Neonatology Pocket Guide: Developmental Delay Evaluation
AAP developmental surveillance and screening guidance (2020)

changelog.change: Initial entry — hard red flags, common normal variants, and the stepwise evaluation.

purpose: Separate the hard red flags (which prompt evaluation whichever milestone framework you use) from the common normal variants, then run the four-step work-up. Loss of previously acquired skills is ALWAYS abnormal.

body.text: Regression — loss of a previously acquired skill at any age — is always abnormal and needs prompt neurology/genetics/metabolic evaluation (consider a neurodegenerative or metabolic disorder, epileptic encephalopathy, or autism with regression).
Red flags (evaluate regardless of milestone framework)

items: Not sitting without support by 9 months.
No hand-to-hand transfer of objects by 12 months.
Abnormal grasp (raking, not pincer) by 15 months.
Loss of any previously acquired skill, at any age.
Nystagmus at any age; persistent hand preference before 12–18 months (suggests a contralateral hemiparesis).
Intermittent strabismus until ~ 4 months (persistent beyond 4 months → ophthalmology).
Toe walking up to ~ 3 years, if passively correctable and there are no other neurological signs.
Developmental (physiologic) speech disfluency up to ~ 4 years.
1. Confirm the delay — structured history, full examination, and a formal standardised screening tool (ASQ-3, M-CHAT for autism) — not a milestone checklist alone.

2. Define the affected domain(s) — isolated (one domain, e.g. motor only) vs global (≥ 2 domains). Global delay raises the priority of cerebral palsy, hypothyroidism, a genetic syndrome, or a metabolic disorder.

3. Search for a cause — review the newborn metabolic screen and growth chart, formal vision and hearing testing; then, guided by the picture: chromosomal microarray + Fragile X, targeted metabolic labs, thyroid function, creatine kinase (for a boy with motor delay — Duchenne), and MRI brain for global delay, microcephaly/macrocephaly, focal findings, seizures, or regression.
4. Manage in parallel with the work-up — refer to early-intervention services immediately (do not wait for a diagnosis), start targeted PT/OT/speech therapy, and arrange educational support.

buildNote: Red flags + normal variants + the 4-step work-up; screening tools named, not milestone checklists.
